subject: Archaeology
title: The Curse of the Pharaohs
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Curse of the Pharaohs.

hook.text: When Lord Carnarvon died weeks after opening Tutankhamun's tomb, newspapers declared a pharaoh's curse.

buildup.text: A cobra ate Howard Carter's pet canary the day the tomb opened. The press went wild with curse stories.

discovery.text: Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite, not a curse. He had been in poor health for years.

twist.text: Howard Carter himself lived until 1939 — 17 years after opening the tomb. The curse skipped him entirely.

climax.text: Studies show that people who entered the tomb lived just as long as those who did not. No curse effect at all.

punchline.text: The pharaoh's curse was real — for newspaper sales.

quiz.question: What actually killed Lord Carnarvon after the tomb opening?
options: Toxic mold spores released from the sealed chamber
An infected mosquito bite, worsened by his poor health
A mysterious illness that doctors could never diagnose

details.summary: The curse of the pharaohs is a myth claiming that those who disturbed Tutankhamun's tomb died mysteriously. Lord Carnarvon's death from an infected mosquito bite fueled newspaper sensationalism, but most expedition members lived long, healthy lives afterward.
details.whyItMatters: The curse myth reveals how media sensationalism shapes public perception of archaeology. It demonstrates the tension between scientific discovery and popular superstition that archaeologists still navigate today.
takeaways: The curse myth began with Lord Carnarvon's death in 1923
Most tomb expedition members lived normal lifespans
Media sensationalism created and sustained the myth

faq.question: Did anyone actually die from the curse?
faq.answer: Lord Carnarvon died from an infected mosquito bite months after the tomb opening. Howard Carter, who opened the tomb himself, lived until 1939 — seventeen years later. Statistical analysis shows expedition members had normal life expectancies.

faq.question: Could toxic mold in the tomb have caused illness?
faq.answer: Some researchers found Aspergillus mold spores in Egyptian tombs that could cause respiratory illness. However, concentrations were too low to cause death, and no expedition members reported mold-related symptoms. The mold theory does not support the curse narrative.
